title: Course 11 Introduction to PySpark - Architecture Runtime Map
subtitle: How PySpark jobs are scheduled, planned, executed, logged, and supported

nodes.label: PySpark Script
nodes.definition: The Python code that defines the Spark job logic.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is where transformation logic and data-processing intent are expressed.
nodes.safeSentence: A PySpark script defines job logic through Python APIs over Spark.
nodes.commonTrap: Thinking script correctness alone guarantees distributed runtime success.

note.summary: PySpark script is the authoring layer for Spark jobs.

nodes.label: Airflow / Scheduler
nodes.definition: Schedules and coordinates jobs, dependencies, parameters, retries, and alerts. It does not perform Spark distributed execution itself.
nodes.whyItMatters: It governs operational timing, dependency control, and alerting in production.
nodes.safeSentence: Airflow orchestrates job flow; Spark handles distributed computation.
nodes.commonTrap: Confusing orchestration tooling with Spark execution internals.

note.summary: Scheduler manages workflow control, not Spark compute internals.

nodes.label: Airflow DAG
nodes.definition: A workflow dependency graph that controls job order, scheduling, retries, parameters, and alerting.
nodes.whyItMatters: It defines pipeline orchestration behavior and reliability expectations.
nodes.safeSentence: An Airflow DAG defines workflow order and operational controls for job runs.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming Airflow DAG and Spark DAG are the same object.

note.summary: Airflow DAG is orchestration logic, not Spark compute plan.

nodes.label: Spark Submit / Job Start
nodes.definition: The mechanism that starts the Spark application and connects it to the runtime environment.
nodes.whyItMatters: Launch configuration controls resources, runtime context, and job behavior.
nodes.safeSentence: Spark submit starts the application with runtime configuration and dependencies.
nodes.commonTrap: Ignoring launch parameters and environment mismatches.

note.summary: Job start bridges orchestration and Spark runtime execution.

nodes.label: Driver Program
nodes.definition: Coordinates the Spark application, builds the plan, and sends tasks to executors.
nodes.whyItMatters: The driver is central to planning, scheduling, and task dispatch.
nodes.safeSentence: The driver coordinates Spark planning and dispatches work to executors.
nodes.commonTrap: Thinking the driver runs all partition-level processing itself.

note.summary: Driver is the control plane for Spark job execution.

nodes.label: Spark DAG
nodes.definition: Spark's internal execution plan built from transformations. Actions trigger it. This is different from an Airflow DAG.
nodes.whyItMatters: It explains stage planning, execution order, and performance behavior.
nodes.safeSentence: Spark DAG is Spark's internal execution graph, different from Airflow workflow DAGs.
nodes.commonTrap: Using DAG terminology without distinguishing Spark planning vs Airflow orchestration.

note.summary: Spark DAG models compute stages inside Spark, not scheduler workflow.

nodes.label: Catalyst Optimizer
nodes.definition: Spark SQL/DataFrame optimizer that rewrites logical plans into efficient physical plans.
nodes.whyItMatters: It affects physical execution shape, shuffle volume, and performance.
nodes.safeSentence: Catalyst rewrites logical DataFrame/SQL plans into optimized physical plans.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming written code order equals physical plan behavior.

note.summary: Catalyst transforms intent into efficient execution strategy.

nodes.label: JVM / Spark Engine
nodes.definition: PySpark gives the developer a Python API, but Spark's core execution engine runs on the JVM.
nodes.whyItMatters: It clarifies safe interview language about Python interface vs engine internals.
nodes.safeSentence: PySpark is a Python interface, with Spark/JVM execution underneath.
nodes.commonTrap: Saying PySpark jobs execute only as pure Python runtime work.

note.summary: Python authors job logic; Spark JVM engine executes distributed core work.

nodes.label: Executors
nodes.definition: Worker processes that run tasks on partitions of data.
nodes.whyItMatters: Executor health and resources drive runtime stability and throughput.
nodes.safeSentence: Executors process partitioned tasks in parallel across cluster resources.
nodes.commonTrap: Ignoring executor memory and failure patterns during troubleshooting.

note.summary: Executors are distributed workers for task execution.

nodes.label: Tasks and Partitions
nodes.definition: Partitions split the data; tasks process partitions in parallel.
nodes.whyItMatters: Partition strategy impacts parallelism, skew risk, and runtime efficiency.
nodes.safeSentence: Tasks run on partitions so data can be processed in parallel.
nodes.commonTrap: Neglecting partition sizing and skew effects.

note.summary: Partitioning defines how work is split across executors.

nodes.label: Shuffle
nodes.definition: Expensive movement of data across executors, often caused by joins, groupBy, repartitioning, and aggregations.
nodes.whyItMatters: Shuffle drives major cost, latency, and failure pressure in distributed jobs.
nodes.safeSentence: Shuffle is cross-executor data movement and should be controlled carefully.
nodes.commonTrap: Ignoring shuffle-heavy operations when analyzing performance problems.

note.summary: Shuffle is necessary for many operations but can be expensive.

nodes.label: Logs, Failure, and Rerun
nodes.definition: Production support view: check logs, failed stages, input/output counts, parameters, dependencies, and rerun safety.
nodes.whyItMatters: Operational reliability depends on disciplined diagnostics and safe rerun patterns.
nodes.safeSentence: Support-ready PySpark includes logging, diagnostics, dependency checks, and safe rerun behavior.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming one successful run means production-grade stability.

note.summary: Production support requires observability and controlled recovery workflows.
